nhiip-india-corridor-land-acquisition.confidence_note: The project's own figures - 775 acres, 11,138 project-affected people, 6,390 structures - remain the World Bank's, from its completion report of 29 June 2022 and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 21 February 2023, and no outside document carries them. What has now been found outside the lender is land acquisition harm on a named corridor of this project. The card previously said that no court record about land acquisition under this project was found and that records of Bihar highway land disputes named no section financed by this loan; both statements are wrong. The Patna High Court and the Central Administrative Tribunal have records on NH-106 Birpur-Bihpur, which the tribunal's judgment of 10 September 2026 describes in the ministry's words as being under Phase-I of the National Highway Interconnectivity Improvement Projects, and for which the Bank published an environmental impact assessment under project number P121185 in February 2014. Those records show one landowner whose land was taken and the road built with no compensation paid, a writ that sat nine years before being sent to a civil court, an arbitration award of Rs 3,66,61,312 unpaid after an execution order, and a dispute over land valued as residential rather than commercial. What is still unsettled is whether the civil works on NH-106 were paid for out of loan IBRD-83010 or, after the 2020 transfer, out of the Green National Highway Corridors Project: the completion report names only the eight sections finished under the loan and does not name NH-106 or any of the five roads in Bihar and West Bengal that were transferred, and the court records give no loan number. Nothing found outside the Bank quantifies the compensation delay the Evaluation Group records, and the Evaluation Group's statement that all 11,138 people were compensated is limited to the subprojects completed under the project, which does not include this road.

field_changes.community: The completion report of 29 June 2022 gives the scale: "The project impacted 775 acres of land, including 558 acres of private land, 6390 structures (including 451 CPRs) and 11,138 PAPs", CPRs being common property resources and PAPs project-affected people. It says that at closure "compensation and eligible assistance were duly paid to all PAPs in six of the 11 road corridors", and that the remaining five roads, in Bihar and West Bengal, were transferred to another Bank-funded project, the Green National Highway Corridors Project, where the pending resettlement plan actions would be closely monitored. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 21 February 2023 records that "disbursement of compensation to project-affected people (PAPs) were substantially delayed in several sections but by project closing, all 11,138 PAPs were compensated for land acquisition for the subprojects completed under the project". That statement is limited to the subprojects completed under the project, the same set as the completion report's six of eleven corridors, so the record holds a delay with no length, no date and no number of people attached to it. Both documents record that the land acquisition was mis-sized: the completion report says poor road designs led to inaccurate assessments of land acquisition needs, particularly on four roads in Bihar, and to variations in the numbers of those affected; the Evaluation Group says needs were inaccurately identified for four roads in Bihar because of inadequate road designs, and that road designs were revised to avoid bypasses that required land acquisition. The completion report says that although most of the land acquisition and resettlement for the project's 15 packages was completed on schedule, there were short but challenging sections on all corridors that were time consuming and led to implementation delays, and that although each state public works department had guaranteed land availability before the works began, in practice the entire land was not handed over. It rates social safeguards performance Moderately Satisfactory, and says the variable quality of work by non-governmental organisation consultants in some packages, with weak management of their contracts by the ministry, led to serious implementation delays. The project received 347 grievances and the completion report says all but one were resolved. Neither document gives a count of people relocated, and neither uses the words displaced or relocated. No village or neighbourhood is named. Outside the Bank's own record, Indian courts and a tribunal have dealt repeatedly with land acquisition on NH-106 Birpur-Bihpur in Bihar, a road the Bank published an environmental impact assessment for under this project number in February 2014 ("Birpur - Udakishanganj Section (km 0 to 106) of NH-106 in the State of Bihar"), the assessment saying of the works that "The Project is being financed by World Bank". The Central Administrative Tribunal's Principal Bench, deciding a service matter brought by a Ministry of Road Transport and Highways chief engineer on 10 September 2026 (OA 3193/2025), quotes the ministry's own description of the contract: rehabilitation and upgrading of the "Birpur-Bihpur Section (km 0+000 to km 106+000) of NH-106 in the State of Bihar under Phase-I of National Highway Interconnectivity Improvement Projects (NHIIP)", awarded to IL&FS Engineering and Construction Company Limited by agreement of 27 September 2016 with the work order issued on 3 October 2016. On that road the Patna High Court recorded on 15 September 2025, in a writ filed in 2016 and pending nine years (CWJC 15126 of 2016, Rajeev Kumar Mishra), that the petitioner's 5 katha at Tola Kamalpur in Supaul district had been acquired and National Highway No. 106 from kilometre 0.00 to kilometre 136.00 "constructed without payment of any compensation to him"; the court sent him to a civil court rather than deciding the claim. On 10 September 2024 the same court recorded, in a case where the Nodal Officer, NHIIP, Road Construction Department, Bihar was a respondent (CWJC 13438 of 2024, Smt. Nutan), that an arbitration award for NH-106 land, set by the Commissioner of Koshi Circle in Arbitration Case 31 of 2020, had gone to execution, that the executing court on 8 February 2024 ordered the Executive Engineer at Madhepura to pay the balance of Rs 3,66,61,312 within fifteen days, and that the money had still not been paid. On 14 July 2026 the court took up a claim for the balance of compensation on 0.1990 acre at Madanpur in Madhepura, acquired for NH-106 Birpur-Bihpur and paid for as residential rather than commercial land (CWJC 10131 of 2026, Vijay Kumar). The road itself was still unfinished: in the High Court's own suo motu proceeding (CWJC 320 of 2019) the acting Chief Justice recorded on 18 April 2025 that the contractor had been due to finish by 2 October 2019 and that "only 95.31% of the work has been completed", with no link roads or diversions, so that even the 103 kilometres built was not in use.

corrections: The card's confidence note said that no court record, press report or NGO field research about land acquisition under this project was found. There are at least five court and tribunal records: Patna High Court CWJC 15126 of 2016 (order 15 September 2025), CWJC 13438 of 2024 (10 September 2024), CWJC 10131 of 2026 (14 July 2026), CWJC 4646 of 2020 (6 March 2020), and Central Administrative Tribunal OA 3193/2025 (10 September 2026).

The card's confidence note said that records of land disputes over highway widening in Bihar name no section financed by this loan. The Central Administrative Tribunal's judgment of 10 September 2026 quotes the ministry's own project title placing the Birpur-Bihpur section (km 0+000 to km 106+000) of NH-106 under Phase-I of NHIIP, and the Bank published an environmental impact assessment for that same stretch under project number P121185 in February 2014. The Patna High Court's suo motu order of 18 April 2025 uses the same description.

The card lists the eight sections the completion report says were built and notes that the five transferred roads are unnamed. One of the project's Bihar roads can now be named from outside documents: NH-106 Birpur-Bihpur, 106 km, contractor IL&FS Engineering and Construction Company Limited, agreement of 27 September 2016, work due to finish 2 October 2019 and still 95.31 per cent complete in April 2025. The Bank's completion report, which closes the account at 2020-2022, carries none of that.

The compensation delay the card reports as having 'no length, no date and no number of people attached to it' now has instances with dates: a writ over an uncompensated taking filed in 2016 and still undecided in September 2025, and an arbitration award for NH-106 land unpaid after an execution order of 8 February 2024.
nhiip-india-corridor-land-acquisition.what_the_outside_source_settles: That land was acquired for a corridor the ministry itself places under Phase-I of this project, that at least one owner's land was taken and the road built with no compensation paid to him, that compensation awards and arbitration awards for NH-106 land were going unpaid years after the loan closed, and that the works on that road were still unfinished in April 2025. It also names the road, the contractor, the contract dates and the districts (Supaul, Madhepura, Saharsa), none of which the Bank's documents do.
nhiip-india-corridor-land-acquisition.what_it_does_not_settle: Whether loan IBRD-83010 paid for the NH-106 civil works, or whether the road was one of the five transferred in 2020 to the Green National Highway Corridors Project, so that the money behind the works had changed hands by the time the court records were made. No court record gives a loan or credit number. None of the project-wide figures - 775 acres, 558 acres private, 6,390 structures, 11,138 project-affected people, 347 grievances - is confirmed by anything outside the Bank, and no outside source gives a count of people relocated or contradicts the zero in the killed field. The three compensation cases concern individual parcels; nothing found says how many owners on this corridor went unpaid.

kisip-informal-settlements-fatalities.confidence_note: The six deaths, the failure to report them to the Bank and the unfinished resettlement of the 82 households are still stated only in the World Bank's own completion report, which also rates the project's outcome satisfactory. The card previously said that a search for independent reporting or litigation on harms under this project found none; that is wrong. Kenya Law's index carries two judgments with the project itself as first respondent - Obul & 4 others, High Court, 15 November 2019, whose petitioners are described as residents of Kopere Market, and Jaramba & 2 others, Environment and Land Court, 19 November 2021 - and a 2025 Environment and Land Court petition brought for 31 families at the riparian section of the Majengo/Talai Settlement Scheme in Kericho, the settlement the completion report names as one where 82 households were still to be moved. The text of all three is behind a JavaScript challenge on Kenya Law's judgment pages, so what they decided, and whether they concern the harms on this card, is not known here. Kenya's Auditor-General audits of the project (years ended 30 June 2020, 2021, 2022 and 2024) are an outside record of the money and confirm the credit numbers and the dates of the financing agreements, but the two that were read record nothing about deaths, resettlement or compensation arrears: the 2020 audit is unqualified and the 2022 audit is qualified only over unsupported travel and subsistence spending. So the deaths remain a lender-only fact, and the count of six rests on one paragraph of one World Bank document.

field_changes.community: The Bank's completion report says the infrastructure component had about 30,000 project-affected persons, roughly 2 per cent of its beneficiaries, and the tenure component about 18,000, roughly 14 per cent. It says all displacement was in-situ, inside the settlement, 'except for three settlements in Kericho and Mombasa (Kwa Hakatsa, Mwatate and Majengo Talai) where alternative land was required to resettle 82 households (328 PAPs) as they were living on environmentally fragile areas and could not be settled in-situ'. At project closing that move had not happened: land had been identified in Mombasa and the planning and resettlement process had begun, and two options for land were still being explored in Kericho. Of about 70 resettlement plans needed where tenure work caused displacement, about 61 had been cleared and about 40 had been implemented or nearly implemented when the completion report was written; no document found counts the people moved under them. The grievance system handled complaints at settlement, county and national level. Separately, the report records deaths on the project's works. Writing of 'the five fatality cases that were related to KISIP, which took place in 2015 and 2018', it says the issue was first identified from a review of a monthly progress report and that during an October 2018 mission, after the Bank asked the client to confirm all incidents involving the project's works or vehicles, 'the Bank team learned that six fatalities had occurred'. It says that although there was awareness at local level to report severe injuries and deaths to resident engineers, contractors and the police, 'there was a systemic failure of reporting to KISIP high level management and to the World Bank'. Three things about this project sit on an outside record. Kenya's Auditor-General has audited the project's accounts year by year under its own credit numbers: the report for the year ended 30 June 2020, the year the credit closed, gives an unqualified opinion and confirms the financing agreements with the International Development Association (No. 4873-KE), the Agence Francaise de Developpement (CKE 1055 01 J) and Sida (TF-018327), dated 23 May 2011, 17 December 2015 and 7 July 2015; it records neither a death on the works nor any outstanding compensation, and the Report on Lawfulness and Effectiveness in Use of Public Resources says nothing came to the Auditor-General's attention to suggest public money was not applied lawfully. The report for the year ended 30 June 2022, signed 13 April 2023, qualifies the accounts on a different matter: Kshs 15,203,347 of goods and services, including Kshs 478,850 of imprest paid to staff on 28 and 30 June 2022 without supporting surrenders and Kshs 1,519,600 paid on 24 December 2021 as subsistence allowance for unidentified officers attending infrastructure inspection meetings. Second, people have sued the project. Kenya Law's index carries Mikael Miyawa Obul & 4 others v Kenya Informal Settlements Improvement Project & 4 others, a High Court judgment of 15 November 2019 ([2019] KEHC 1895) whose petitioners the index describes as residents of Kopere Market, Daraja Mbili Township, and Paul Odhiambo Jaramba & 2 others v Kenya Informal Settlements Improvement Project (KISSIP) & 5 others, an Environment and Land Court judgment of 19 November 2021 ([2021] KEELC 855). Kenya Law's index also carries an earlier ruling in the same dispute, Michael Miyawa Obul & 4 others v Kenya Informal Settlements & 4 others [2018] KEHC 4492, a constitutional petition in the High Court at Kisumu decided on 30 August 2018 with the project as first respondent, and the index snippet for the 2019 judgment says the Informal Settlements Improvement Project "was being undertaken at Kopere Market". Third, at Majengo Talai in Kericho, one of the three settlements where the Bank's completion report says 82 households had to be moved off environmentally fragile land and had not been moved by closing, the Environment and Land Court was still hearing the matter in 2025: Mutai & 4 others, who the case title says represent 31 families or squatters at the riparian section in the Majengo/Talai Settlement Scheme, against the Kericho County Government and four others (Constitutional Petition E001 of 2025, ruling of 11 December 2025), a case the index shows turning on a multi-agency task force and "lists of squatters in Majengo/Talai Settlement Scheme prepared by KISIP". The text of those three judgments could not be read: Kenya Law's judgment pages are behind a JavaScript challenge that plain requests cannot pass, so only the index entries and the snippets its search interface returns are reported here.

assam-roads-uncompensated-acquisition.confidence_note: The harm on this card - land and property taken for this project without paying the owners - is now on a court record outside the lender. Three Gauhati High Court orders deal with acquisition for the project's State Highway 2 upgrading towards Barpeta, which the completion report's own table names as SH-02 Chapaguri-Manas-Barpeta, and they name the owners, the villages, the dags and pattas, the Land Acquisition Case numbers and the dates. In Amzad Hussain and 2 others (WP(C) 5103/2016, 29 April 2022) three owners at Bartari were called in to collect compensation and paid nothing, and the court found no reason had been given for the non-payment; the money was still unpaid two and a half years after the loan closed. In Hakim Mullah (WP(C) 2114/2021, 23 March 2022) the award for land at Jahorupam, acquired in Land Acquisition Case 1/2011-12, left the patta holders out and nothing had been disbursed. In Saidul Islam (WP(C) 5699/2024, 8 November 2024) the heirs of a pattadar at Kandulia were left off the beneficiary list of 5 September 2020 and the compensation for their share went to relatives. What the court record does not settle is whether these claimants were on the package the Bank says it suspended: the Bank names no package, no corridor, no district and no owner, so the two accounts cannot be matched person to person, and in two of the three cases the failure is that money was paid to the wrong people rather than not raised at all. The project team's statement to the evaluators that all compensation was fully paid and all land acquisition issues amicably settled is contradicted for at least these owners, whose claims were live in 2022 and 2024.

field_changes.community: The project upgraded and rehabilitated roads in Assam, 978 km by closing against a revised target of 1,000 km. At appraisal, social screening covered about 420 km of roads, with a census and socio-economic survey of the people in every structure and on all land within the corridor of impact for Phase I of the upgrading component. The assessment concluded that widening to two lanes would not need extensive resettlement because the work would mostly stay inside the existing right of way, and that about 80 per cent of the land needed was already available in stretches along the Phase I corridors. On one of the project's packages that broke down. The completion report states plainly that the project departed from the agreements reached under the Resettlement Action Plan and that the land and properties were acquired without paying compensation to the owners. As a corrective measure, work on the affected package was suspended until the required processes were completed and the compensation funds were transferred. The completion report says compensation was otherwise largely paid on time, 'barring for one package'. The completion report records the remaining activity of compensation payment for land acquisition as settled, confirmed by the completion report mission. The Independent Evaluation Group repeats the episode and adds what the project team told it by email on 10 June 2020: that for the first three years no designated staff was involved in the land acquisition process, and that after the department strengthened its environment and social cell in the second half of the project 'all the compensation was fully paid, and all the land acquisition issues were amicably settled'. The project also could not obtain utilisation certificates for money spent on land acquisition and utility shifting by other state agencies, which the state met from its own funds, and the project's financial management rating was lowered to unsatisfactory for a year after it took two years to answer the Auditor General's inspection report. The policy on indigenous peoples was triggered at appraisal because some corridors were expected to pass through areas where indigenous communities had settled, and an Indigenous Peoples Development Plan was prepared, but the completion report states the policy was never applied during implementation because the project did not pass through any major tribal settlements. The package is not named in any Bank document, but the Gauhati High Court has a run of cases about acquisition for one of the project's upgrading stretches, State Highway 2 towards Barpeta - the completion report's own economic table lists SH-02 Chapaguri-Manas-Barpeta, 60.52 km, among the six upgrading roads. The court's orders describe the works as the "double lining of existing carriageway under the Assam State Road Project - portion from Langla to Barpeta Town", acquired in Land Acquisition Cases 1/2011-12 and 9/2011-2012 under the Land Acquisition Act 1894; in Case 9/2011-2012 the section 4 notification was published on 25 July 2012 and the section 6 declaration on 30 May 2013. In Amzad Hussain and 2 others v The State of Assam and 4 others (WP(C) 5103/2016, order of 29 April 2022), in which the Project Director of the Assam State Roads Project is the third respondent, three owners of patta land at Bartari, Mouza Titapani in Barpeta district were served notices to come and collect compensation, attended, and were paid nothing; the Circle Officer's affidavit accepted that the land was theirs and that payment had been suspended because of another landowners' writ, which had been withdrawn on 18 February 2019. The court held that "no reasons have been furnished as to why compensation due has not been paid" and gave the Deputy Commissioner four months to verify and release it - six years after the owners' representation of 7 April 2016 and two and a half years after the loan closed. In Hakim Mullah v The State of Assam and 10 others (WP(C) 2114/2021, order of 23 March 2022) the petitioner's 4 kathas 7 lechas at Jahorupam, Mouza Ghilajari in Barpeta had been acquired in Land Acquisition Case 1/2011-12 and the award made, but the pattadars' names were left out of the award statement in favour of the occupiers, and "such land acquisition compensation has not yet been disbursed" to either side; a compensation sum of Rs 9,84,936 was about to be released to the occupiers. The court sent the apportionment to the District Judge under section 30. In Saidul Islam v The State of Assam and 4 others (WP(C) 5699/2024, order of 8 November 2024) the heirs of a man whose land at Kandulia, Mouza Titapani fell inside Land Acquisition Case 9/2011-2012 were left off the beneficiary list of 5 September 2020 and the whole compensation for their plot was paid to relatives; the court sent them to a civil court. A fourth case, M/S Super Infratech Pte Ltd v The State of Assam and 4 others (WP(C) 6047/2015, order of 20 September 2019), is a contractor's matter but names the respondent as "Assam State Road Projects, represented by the Project Director, World Bank Aided Projects, P.W.R.D.", which is how the project appears on the court record.

corrections: The card says no independent account was found and that the documents do not name the package, the corridor, the district or the owners. The corridor and district can now be named from the court record: the double-laning of State Highway 2 from Langla to Barpeta Town in Barpeta district, which the completion report's economic annex lists as SH-02 Chapaguri-Manas-Barpeta, 60.52 km, acquired in Land Acquisition Cases 1/2011-12 and 9/2011-2012; the section 4 notification in Case 9/2011-2012 was published on 25 July 2012 and the section 6 declaration on 30 May 2013. Named owners include Amzad Hussain, Amjad Ali Mondal and Abdul Kayam of Bartari, Hakim Mullah of Jahorupam and the heirs of Amiruddin of Kandulia.

The project team told the Independent Evaluation Group by email on 10 June 2020 that all the compensation was fully paid and all land acquisition issues amicably settled. On 29 April 2022 the Gauhati High Court was still directing the Deputy Commissioner, Barpeta to verify and release compensation to three owners whose land had been acquired, and on 23 March 2022 it recorded that the award money in Land Acquisition Case 1/2011-12 had not been disbursed to the patta holders. On 8 November 2024 it heard a further claim on the same acquisition. The claim of full settlement does not survive those orders.

The card's note that the documents do not say how long any owner went unpaid can be answered in part: the Bartari owners' representation to the Deputy Commissioner is dated 7 April 2016 and the court was still ordering release on 29 April 2022, six years later; the Jahorupam petitioner's representation is dated 7 March 2017 and nothing had been paid by 23 March 2022.
assam-roads-uncompensated-acquisition.what_the_outside_source_settles: That land acquired for this project's State Highway 2 upgrading in Barpeta district went unpaid for years, with the owners, parcels, Land Acquisition Case numbers, notification dates and sums on the record of the Gauhati High Court, and that the project's own Project Director was a respondent in one of the cases. It puts the harm on an outside record and dates it, and it contradicts the project team's closing statement that everything had been settled.
assam-roads-uncompensated-acquisition.what_it_does_not_settle: Whether these are the owners of the package the Bank suspended. The Bank names no package, so the identification runs through the works rather than the parties: the court orders name the Assam State Road Project and State Highway 2 to Barpeta, which the completion report's table lists as a project stretch, but nothing ties these particular claimants to the suspension or to the compensation funds the Bank says were transferred. In two of the three cases the complaint is that the award money went to occupiers or relatives rather than to the patta holders, which is an apportionment failure as well as a non-payment. No outside document gives a count of owners affected, a count of people relocated, or any figure for the money eventually paid; the card's displaced field stays empty and ICIJ's 2,891 is still unexplained.
